title: Going Underground and Going Electric
summary: London's streets were so jammed that engineers put a railway in a tunnel underneath, first with smoky steam engines. Then inventors learned to run trains on electricity, with no smoke at all. Soon cities from Budapest to New York to Moscow had trains rumbling beneath their feet.

sections.heading: A City Too Crowded to Move
paragraphs: Imagine London in the 1850s. It is the biggest city in the world, with well over two million people. Railways from all over Britain now bring passengers into the capital, but Parliament has not allowed the main lines to push into the crowded centre, so their stations, such as Paddington, Euston and King's Cross, sit around the edge. Every morning thousands of passengers pour out and try to cross town to their offices in the City of London. The streets are choked with horse-drawn buses, cabs, carts and pedestrians. A trip of a couple of miles could take longer than the whole train journey that came before it.

A London lawyer named Charles Pearson had a bold answer: put a railway underneath the streets. He spent years campaigning for the idea, and the engineer John Fowler was put in charge of designing it. Many people thought it was mad. Who would want to ride through a dark tunnel, breathing smoke, under the houses of London? Some newspapers joked about it, and some people worried the tunnels would collapse or that being underground was simply unhealthy. Pearson sadly died in September 1862, just a few months before his dream opened.

The new line was called the Metropolitan Railway. It was built mostly by a method called 'cut-and-cover'. Workers dug an enormous trench down the middle of a street, built the railway in the bottom, lined the sides with brick walls, covered the top with a brick arch or iron girders, and then rebuilt the road on top. It was quick compared with real tunnelling, but it turned streets into building sites for months, and houses that stood in the way sometimes had to be knocked down. Where possible, the route followed the line of existing roads, such as the New Road (today's Marylebone Road and Euston Road), so that fewer buildings had to be demolished.

After a grand opening ceremony on 9 January 1863, the Metropolitan Railway opened to the public on 10 January 1863. It ran about 3.75 miles (6 km) from Paddington (Bishop's Road) to Farringdon Street, near the City. It was the world's first underground railway. About 38,000 passengers rode it on the very first day, so many that extra trains had to be borrowed, and around 9.5 million people used it in its first year. The doubters had been wrong: Londoners loved it.

sections.heading: Steam in the Tunnels
paragraphs: There was one big problem. In 1863 the only practical way to pull a train was a steam locomotive, and steam locomotives burn coal, make smoke and puff out steam. In the open air, the smoke just blows away. In a tunnel, it has nowhere to go.

The engineers had tried to plan for this. The track was laid with three rails so that both broad-gauge trains of the Great Western Railway and standard-gauge trains could use it, and the first trains were pulled by special Great Western tank engines. Later the Metropolitan used its own locomotives fitted with 'condensing' equipment: instead of blasting used steam up the chimney, the engine sent it back into its water tanks, where it cooled and turned back into water. Drivers were also told to burn coke or smokeless fuel in the tunnels and to stoke the fire hard only in the open sections between them.

It helped, but not enough. The original line had very little ventilation, because it had been designed hoping that smokeless engines would be found. Stations and carriages were often hazy with sulphurous smoke, and the air tasted of soot. Passengers rode in gas-lit wooden carriages, and on busy days the atmosphere could be choking. Over the years, the company opened up vents and gaps in the roof to let smoke out, sometimes to the annoyance of people living above. Some people of the time even claimed the sulphur-filled air was good for chest complaints, which almost certainly was not true.

Even so, the 'sub-surface' network kept growing, linking up to form what eventually became the Circle line. But it was obvious that underground railways needed a cleaner way to move. If only you could have an engine that produced no smoke at all. The answer was already being tested in workshops and exhibitions across Europe: electricity.

sections.heading: Sparks in Berlin and Brighton
paragraphs: Electric motors had existed since the 1830s, but early ones were weak and depended on batteries, which were expensive and quickly ran down. By the 1870s that changed. Engineers built powerful dynamos, machines that turn movement into electricity, and the same machine run in reverse could work as a motor. Now electricity could be made in large amounts and sent along wires.

The German inventor Werner von Siemens, whose company Siemens and Halske was a leader in telegraphs and electrical machines, saw the chance. At the Berlin trade exhibition of 1879 he presented a little electric locomotive on 31 May. It ran on a loop of track about 300 metres long, with a gauge of just 490 millimetres, pulling three small open cars that each seated six people. It trundled along at about 7 kilometres per hour, not much faster than a brisk walk. Electricity at 150 volts reached it through the two running rails and a separate iron strip laid between them, and the locomotive picked up power with sliding contacts. By 30 September 1879 it had carried 86,398 riders, who were thrilled to be pulled along by an engine with no fire and no smoke. It is often called the world's first electric passenger train.

Siemens kept going. In May 1881 his company opened the world's first electric tram service in Gross-Lichterfelde, a suburb of Berlin. Trams (called streetcars or trolleys in North America) are lighter railways that run along city streets. Before electricity, most of them were pulled by horses, which were expensive to feed, got tired, fell ill and left the streets covered in manure. Electric trams spread quickly from the 1880s onwards and soon replaced horse trams in cities around the world.

Meanwhile, in the English seaside resort of Brighton, an inventor named Magnus Volk opened a tiny electric railway along the beach in August 1883. The first section was only about a quarter of a mile long, ran on track 2 feet (610 millimetres) wide, and used just 50 volts of electricity. Volk was already known locally for his electrical experiments, including early attempts at electric lighting in the home. His railway was extended and rebuilt over the years, and it is still running today along about a mile of seafront. That makes Volk's Electric Railway the oldest electric railway in the world that still operates, even though it was not the first one ever built.

Volk was full of ideas. In 1896 he opened a strange railway that ran through the shallow sea itself. Its carriage stood on long legs about 7 metres high, so it rolled along rails on the seabed while passengers rode above the waves. People nicknamed it 'Daddy Long Legs'. It closed around 1900, after only a few years, but it shows how excited and inventive people were about the new power.

sections.heading: Into the Deep: The First Electric Tube
paragraphs: Cut-and-cover had a serious limit. It only worked a few metres below the surface, under wide streets, and it tore up the city while it was being built. To go under buildings, under the River Thames and deep beneath the crowded City of London, engineers needed to bore real tunnels through the London clay, far below the cellars and sewers.

The key tool was the tunnelling shield, improved by the engineer James Henry Greathead. Picture a giant steel tube, a little wider than the tunnel, pushed forward into the clay by powerful hydraulic jacks. Men worked inside the front of the shield, digging out the clay, while the shield protected them from collapses. As it inched forward, workers bolted rings of curved cast-iron segments together behind it to form the tunnel lining. Ring after ring, the tunnel grew, perfectly round and strong. Greathead had already used this method on a small tunnel under the Thames, and now he used it for a full railway.

That railway was the City and South London Railway. It was first planned to work like San Francisco's cable cars, with carriages gripping a moving cable pulled by engines at the ends of the line. But in 1888 the company supplying the cable system went bankrupt, and the railway's chairman, Charles Grey Mott, made a brave decision: use electricity instead. Nobody had ever run a deep underground railway on electric power before.

The line was officially opened by Edward, Prince of Wales, on 4 November 1890, and it opened to the public on 18 December 1890. It ran about 3.2 miles (5.1 kilometres) from Stockwell, south of the river, under the Thames to King William Street in the City, with six stations. This was the first deep-level 'tube' railway worked by electric trains, the ancestor of today's Northern line.

Riding it was an adventure. Small electric locomotives built by the firm Mather and Platt pulled the trains, taking power at 500 volts from an extra rail beside the track. The tunnels were only about 3.1 metres (10 feet 2 inches) across, so the carriages were small, with high-backed benches and only narrow slits of windows near the roof, since there was nothing to see in a tunnel anyway. Each carriage held about 32 passengers, and people nicknamed them 'padded cells'. There were no tickets and no first or third class: everyone paid a flat fare of two pennies at a turnstile. Since the stations were deep underground, passengers went down in hydraulic lifts.

The little line was slow and cramped, and its locomotives struggled at first, but it proved that deep electric railways worked. More tubes followed. The Central London Railway opened in 1900 and was nicknamed the 'Twopenny Tube' because of its flat two-penny fare. Within a few years, the old smoky Metropolitan Railway also switched to electricity: electric trains began running in 1905, and by 1907 they worked most of its services. The age of steam underground was coming to an end.

Building tubes was hugely expensive, and much of the money for the next wave came from an American businessman, Charles Tyson Yerkes, who had made his fortune with streetcar lines in Chicago. His group finished three new deep tubes in just two years: the line nicknamed the Bakerloo (from Baker Street and Waterloo) in 1906, the Piccadilly line in 1906, and the Hampstead line, part of today's Northern line, in 1907. The different railway companies were rivals at first, but they began to advertise together, and from 1908 their stations carried the same big word 'UNDERGROUND'. The famous red circle with a blue bar, known as the roundel, became the network's symbol, and the companies were finally brought together under one public body, London Transport, in 1933.

That same year, a young engineering draughtsman named Harry Beck produced a new kind of map for the Underground. Instead of showing where the lines really ran, with all their bends and true distances, he drew them as straight lines running only up, down, across or at neat 45-degree angles, with stations evenly spaced, rather like an electrical circuit diagram. Passengers did not need to know exact distances underground; they needed to know which line to take and where to change. Beck's diagram was a huge success, and almost every metro map in the world today follows his idea.

sections.heading: Frank Sprague: Climbing Hills and Coupling Motors
paragraphs: Across the Atlantic, one of the most important figures in electric railways was Frank J. Sprague, a former United States Navy officer who had studied at the Naval Academy. In 1883 he went to work for the famous inventor Thomas Edison, but he left after about a year to start his own company making electric motors. Edison himself later praised Sprague's motor as the most practical one available.

Sprague's big test came in Richmond, Virginia. He agreed to electrify a whole city streetcar system there, the Richmond Union Passenger Railway, which was a risky promise because Richmond is very hilly and the motors of the time often overheated or failed on steep slopes. There were breakdowns and frantic repairs, and the job is said to have cost Sprague far more than he was paid, but on 2 February 1888 passenger service began. It is widely seen as the first large, successful electric street railway system. Cities across America noticed. Within just a few years, hundreds of towns had switched from horse cars to electric streetcars, and horse-drawn trams almost disappeared.

Sprague's second great idea was even more important for trains. Early electric trains were usually pulled by one locomotive, just like steam trains. A locomotive has to be heavy to grip the rails, and all the pulling force comes from one place. Sprague asked: why not put motors under many carriages and control them all from a single driving cab? This is called multiple-unit control.

Here is how it works. Each motor carriage has its own traction motors and its own set of switches. Thin control wires run the whole length of the train, linking all the carriages. When the driver moves the controller in the front cab, signals go down those wires and every carriage's switches respond together, so all the motors start, speed up or slow down at the same moment. One driver can control a long train with dozens of motors as if it were a single machine.

Sprague first tried his system on the South Side Elevated Railroad in Chicago in 1897. The advantages were huge. Because the motors were spread along the train, more wheels were driven, so trains gripped the rails better and could speed up quickly, which is perfect for city lines with stations every few hundred metres. Trains could be made longer or shorter simply by coupling or uncoupling carriages. If one motor failed, the others kept the train moving. And with a driving cab at each end, a train could reverse at the end of the line without the driver needing to move a locomotive around. Almost every metro and suburban electric train in the world today, and many high-speed trains, still use this idea. Sprague also built electric lifts (elevators), which helped make tall city buildings practical, so he changed how people moved both sideways and up and down.

sections.heading: How an Electric Train Works
paragraphs: A steam locomotive carries its own power station on board: fire, boiler and water. An electric train is different. Its energy is made somewhere else, at a power station, and delivered to the train while it moves. That is why an electric train makes no smoke where it runs, which is exactly what tunnels and crowded cities needed. (The power station may still burn fuel and make pollution, but it is far away from passengers, and today more and more electricity comes from wind, solar, hydro and nuclear power.)

There are two main ways to feed electricity to a moving train. The first is a third rail: an extra rail laid on insulated supports beside or between the running rails. A metal 'shoe' sticking out from the train slides along the top or side of this rail and picks up the current, and the current returns through the wheels and running rails, completing the circuit. Third rails usually carry direct current at fairly low voltages, typically up to about 750 volts. They fit neatly inside small tunnels, which made them perfect for subways. London's Underground uses a fourth rail as well, in the middle of the track, to carry the return current, which protects the old metal tunnel linings from slowly corroding. Because a live rail lies close to the ground, it is dangerous to touch, which is why people must never walk on railway tracks.

The second way is an overhead line: wires hung above the track on poles or gantries. On the train's roof sits a pantograph, a folding, springy metal frame that pushes a contact strip up against the wire. (The name comes from an old drawing instrument with a similar folding shape.) Overhead lines can safely carry much higher voltages, such as 25,000 volts alternating current on many modern main lines, because the wire is far above people's heads. Higher voltage means fewer power substations are needed along the route and more power can reach fast, heavy trains, so overhead wires are used for most high-speed railways. Third rails are usually limited to slower trains, roughly up to 160 kilometres per hour.

Once the electricity is on board, it goes to the traction motors, electric motors mounted near the axles that turn the wheels through gears. Inside a motor, electric current flowing through coils of wire creates magnetic forces that push against each other and make a shaft spin. Electric motors have a great strength: they produce strong turning force (called torque) right from a standstill, so electric trains can pull away quickly and smoothly. They are also simpler than steam engines, with far fewer moving parts, no fire to tend and no water to refill.

Many modern electric trains can even run their motors backwards as generators when slowing down. This is called regenerative braking: the train's movement is turned back into electricity and fed into the wires to help power other trains, instead of being wasted as heat in the brakes. A steam engine, which you saw in Part 9 wasted most of its fuel's energy, could never do anything like that.

sections.heading: Subways Spread Around the World
paragraphs: Once London had shown the way, other great cities dug in. In Budapest, the capital of Hungary, a short underground line opened on 2 May 1896 for celebrations marking a thousand years since the Magyars (Hungarians) arrived in the region. It was opened by Emperor Franz Joseph and ran for about 5 kilometres under the elegant Andrássy Avenue to the city park. It was electric from the start, and it is the oldest electric underground railway on mainland Europe. Its small yellow trains still run, and the line has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002. In the same year, Glasgow in Scotland opened its own subway, at first pulled by cables.

On 1 September 1897 Boston opened the Tremont Street Subway, the oldest subway tunnel in North America. It was not a railway for heavy trains but a tunnel for streetcars, built to clear trams off the city's jammed streets. Bostonians crowded in to ride, and parts of the tunnel are still used today, more than 125 years later.

Paris opened Line 1 of its Métro on 19 July 1900, while the city was hosting a huge world's fair, the Exposition Universelle. It ran from Porte Maillot to Porte de Vincennes, right across the city. The engineer Fulgence Bienvenüe, often called the 'father of the Métro', helped plan the whole system as a connected network from the beginning, and the architect Hector Guimard designed beautiful station entrances of curving green ironwork in the Art Nouveau style, looking a bit like strange plants. Eighty-six of them still survive and have become symbols of Paris.

New York had been arguing about subways for more than twenty years. Finally, the Interborough Rapid Transit Company, founded by the financier August Belmont Jr., opened the city's first subway line on 27 October 1904. It ran from City Hall in lower Manhattan up to 145th Street at Broadway. Huge crowds lined up to ride, and the fare was a nickel, five cents. Unlike London's early tubes, New York's subway had separate express tracks so that fast trains could skip local stations. It grew into one of the largest subway systems on Earth.

One of the most famous of all opened on 15 May 1935 in Moscow, the capital of the Soviet Union. Its first line was about 11 kilometres long with 13 stations. The Soviet government wanted the Metro to show off the power of its system, so many stations were built like underground palaces, with marble walls, chandeliers, mosaics and statues, and some were described as bringing an 'artificial underground sun' to the workers. It was built very quickly by huge teams of workers, often in difficult and dangerous conditions. Today the Moscow Metro carries more than two billion passengers a year.

By the 1930s, underground and elevated electric railways had become the beating heart of big cities. Today more than 150 cities around the world have metro systems, from Tokyo and Shanghai to Mexico City and Cairo, nearly all of them electric and nearly all using Sprague's idea of motors spread along the train. Yet out on the long main lines across the countryside, where stringing up wires for thousands of miles was very expensive, the steam locomotive still ruled. Above ground, an engine invented by a German engineer named Rudolf Diesel was about to challenge the mighty steam locomotive.

deepDive: Why did electricity take so long to win, if it was so much cleaner? Part of the answer is cost. An electric railway needs a whole hidden system before a single train moves: power stations, cables, substations to convert or step down the voltage, and either a third rail or overhead wires along every metre of track. For a busy city line carrying trains every few minutes, that investment pays off quickly. For a country line with a few trains a day, it often does not. That is why cities electrified first, while many main lines kept steam and later switched to diesel. Another debate was over which kind of electricity to use. Early systems used direct current (DC), which suited the motors of the time well and is still used on most metros, usually at 600 to 750 volts, or at 1,500 or 3,000 volts on some main lines. But DC is hard to send long distances, because low voltage means high current, and high current wastes energy as heat in the wires. Alternating current (AC) can be stepped up to high voltage with transformers for efficient transmission, then stepped down on the train. After the Second World War, improved equipment made 25,000-volt AC at 50 hertz (the same frequency as the public power grid in many countries) the favourite for new main lines, starting with experiments in France. Some countries, such as Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Sweden and Norway, use 15,000 volts at a special lower frequency of 16.7 hertz, a choice made in the early 1900s when motors could not cope with higher frequencies. Historians also debate 'firsts'. Siemens's 1879 exhibition loop carried passengers but was a demonstration; Volk's 1883 line is the oldest still running; the Gross-Lichterfelde tram of 1881 was the first regular public electric tram; and the City and South London of 1890 was the first deep-level electric tube. There were also important early electric experiments in the United States, by inventors such as Leo Daft and Charles Van Depoele, before Sprague's Richmond success in 1888. As with steam, electric traction grew out of many inventors improving one another's work, rather than a single genius.
funFact: Volk's Electric Railway in Brighton opened in 1883 and still carries passengers along the seafront today, making it the oldest operating electric railway in the world.
